clue.text: Bear reacts with fury — this lasts less time than the others

definitions.text: this lasts less time than the others

indicators.note: substances that react with each other combine into something new, so the words either side are blended and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry bear lashes out, though its rage blows over sooner than that of the other animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reacts with' is the anagram signal, blending BEAR and FURY. The definition is a riddle about the calendar: one month is shorter than the other eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: Riddle-style description: it is the shortest month, with 28 days, or 29 in a leap year, against 30 or 31 for the rest.

clue.text: Not stay firm without sacred text — I will fall

parts.note: w/o is a standard written abbreviation of without

indicators.note: something that will fall drops away: the letter named just before these words is lost from the sacred text

parts.note: the Bible is the holy book of Christianity
taken as written

explanation.surface: A believer admits that, deprived of scripture, their resolve gives way and they stumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will fall' takes I out of BIBLE, leaving BBLE. 'without' looks like the removal signal, but it only supplies WO, from the shorthand w/o.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonymous verb phrase: something unsteady that rocks from side to side is failing to hold steady.

clue.text: Hen or duck's no fine bird

indicators.note: having no fine means the letter for fine is absent, so it is struck from the poultry word

parts.note: a hen and a duck are both fowl, birds kept for their eggs or meat; the 's stands for has
F is the abbreviation for fine, as in the grades of pencil lead

explanation.surface: A hen, or even a duck, is dismissed as not much of a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the 's as 'has': the word for a hen or duck has 'no' F, and losing that letter leaves a quite different bird, one that hunts at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: a nocturnal hunter with large forward-facing eyes.

clue.text: Animal wants limb freed, catching end of foot in this?

indicators.note: the run of three pieces catches the picked letter, taking it in among its own letters
to want is to need: the animal needs the next two pieces set down after it

parts.note: a cat is an animal
a leg is a limb
rid means freed, as in being rid of a burden

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A trapped creature struggles to pull its leg loose after its hoof gets stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay doubles as a description of 'this': a barred pit in a road, where a hoof could stick. 'wants' attaches the freed limb to the animal, 'catching' takes a letter in, and 'end of' picks that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The surface is the description: bars laid over a pit in a road, which livestock will not cross because a hoof would slip through; Americans say cattle guard.

clue.text: Call for soldiers, some of them by place of death, as heard in poem

parts.note: them points back to the soldiers: the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE, are a corps of the British Army

indicators.note: heard asks for the sound of a word, not its spelling, and in poem says the place of death is one named in a famous poem

parts.note: in Tennyson's The Charge of the Light Brigade the six hundred ride 'into the valley of Death'

explanation.surface: A bugle summons troops, some of them posted near a spot where men died, as a poem tells it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as heard in poem' asks for the sound of Tennyson's 'valley of Death', spelt VEILLE; the British say this bugle call 'ri-VALLY', not the American 'REV-uh-lee'. 'some of them' means some soldiers: the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Military term: the bugle or drum signal that wakes troops in the morning.

clue.text: Argument during lunch

parts.note: a tiff is a petty quarrel
in can mean during, as in 'in the night'

explanation.surface: A row breaks out over the midday meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' looks like an instruction to put one piece inside another, but it is only a synonym here. The answer is an Anglo-Indian word, familiar in Britain from the days of the Raj.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo-Indian word for a light midday meal, still current in India and in old-fashioned British English.

clue.text: Instrument not in tune leader refused

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and refusing it means leaving that letter off

parts.note: a note that is sharp is pitched slightly too high, so it is out of tune

explanation.surface: An orchestra's leader turns away an instrument that is off pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader refused' drops the first letter of SHARP. In the surface the leader is a person, the principal violinist of a British orchestra, rejecting an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: a tall stringed instrument plucked with the fingers.

clue.text: Unlikely to be imported from the antipodes?

definitions.meaning: said of a story or excuse that is hard to believe
read literally: goods shipped from the antipodes, the British name for Australia and New Zealand, have been brought a very long way

explanation.surface: Goods are not expected to be shipped in from Australia or New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one thought, but it splits after the first word; 'to be' only joins the halves. The question mark flags the second half as a playful, literal reading of the answer's two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym for implausible, and, read literally as two words, a whimsical description of anything brought from the other side of the world.

clue.text: Holding end of loaf that's black, secure somewhere to get rid of it?

definitions.text: somewhere to get rid of it

indicators.note: the word for secure holds the other three pieces inside it; the instruction comes first, ahead of everything it governs

parts.note: to secure a prize or a contract is to win it
the heel is the crusty end slice of a loaf of bread
that is, in Latin id est, is abbreviated i.e.
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone clutching a burnt crust looks for a safe place to throw it away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of loaf' looks like a request for the letter F, but it means the crust itself. 'Holding' is the container signal, and the result is the wheeled household rubbish bin that British councils empty each week.
explanation.definitionFit: British name for the large wheeled household rubbish container, which is where a burnt crust would be thrown away.

clue.text: Operating system said to flop

indicators.note: said tells you to speak the system's name aloud and write down another word that sounds the same

parts.note: DOS, the disk operating system, ran early personal computers and is pronounced as a single word

explanation.surface: A new piece of computer software is tipped to be a commercial failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' asks for the sound of DOS, the old PC operating system. 'Flop' is not a failure here but American slang for bedding down somewhere makeshift, which is what the British call dossing.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonyms: both mean to sleep or bed down somewhere rough or makeshift, one British and the other American.

clue.text: A smile can transform communications

indicators.note: to transform is to change form, so the letters just before these words can be put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, six letters in all

explanation.surface: A friendly grin can change the whole tone of a conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can transform' is the anagram signal for the six letters of A SMILE. The surface is a warm truth about body language; the answer is a more routine kind of message.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural noun for electronic messages, an everyday form of written contact.

clue.text: Auburn, one changing position with hesitation, showing an element of grey

indicators.note: the letter named just before these words leaves its place in the colour word and settles elsewhere in it

parts.note: Titian is a bright reddish-brown hair colour, named after the red-haired women painted by the Venetian artist Titian
I is the Roman numeral for one
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A fidgeting, dithering redhead is starting to show a few grey hairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing position' sends the second I of the hair colour to the end of its word, making TITANI. The surface is about hair going grey; the definition is a chemical element that is grey in colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Description by colour: a strong, light metal, number 22 in the periodic table, that is silvery-grey.

clue.text: Concerned with software to promote? Think again!

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as at the head of a business letter
an app is a piece of software
to raise someone to a higher rank is to promote them

explanation.surface: A worker fretting over which program to push is told to reconsider.
explanation.walkthrough: Three pieces in clue order with no indicator at all; the question mark and the exclamation mark are surface punctuation only.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an instruction: to assess something afresh is to reconsider it.

clue.text: I'm surprised a ditch only goes halfway

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: going only halfway means stopping at the midpoint, so just the first half of the ditch word is used

parts.note: ha-ha is the name for the sunken ditch that bounds an English country-house garden without blocking the view

explanation.surface: The speaker is startled to find that a trench stops partway across the field.
explanation.walkthrough: The ha-ha is a sunken ditch bounding English country-house gardens, keeping livestock out without spoiling the view. 'only goes halfway' keeps the first half of HAHA, after the clue's own A.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamation of sudden discovery or mild astonishment, the sort of thing said on being taken aback.

clue.text: Ignored, not quite like Ethelred?

indicators.note: not quite the whole word is used: it stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: Ethelred the Unready was an English king who died in 1016, so someone like him is unready

explanation.surface: Someone is being overlooked, though not as badly as a hapless Anglo-Saxon king.
explanation.walkthrough: Ethelred the Unready was an Anglo-Saxon king of England, known to British schoolchildren by that nickname. 'not quite' drops the final Y of UNREADY.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: a letter, message or book that nobody has opened has been passed over.

clue.text: Viewers discuss a feature of crustaceans

parts.note: eyes are what we view with, so crosswords call them viewers
to talk something over is to discuss it

explanation.surface: A television audience chats about some part of a crab or lobster's body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewers' suggests a television audience, but here they are the organs of sight. The result is the movable stem that carries the eye of a crab or lobster.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomical term: the movable stem on which the eye of a crab, lobster or shrimp sits.

clue.text: Confounds with question: what's on at the club tonight?

definitions.text: what's on at the club tonight

parts.note: to floor someone is to baffle them completely, as an unexpected question does
how is one of the question words, the one that asks in what way

explanation.surface: Someone stumps the doorman by asking about the evening's entertainment at a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'question' stands for a question word, HOW, not for the question that follows the colon. That question is the definition: the cabaret a nightclub puts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: the cabaret entertainment of singers, dancers or comedians that a nightclub stages.

clue.text: Freedom fighter's pig about to be chopped

indicators.note: the pig word goes about, that is around, the shortened word that follows it

parts.note: a boar is a male pig, or a wild pig

indicators.note: chopping a word cuts off its last letter

parts.note: to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: A rebel's hog is on the point of being butchered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to be' reads as 'on the point of being', but the phrase breaks up: 'about' is the container signal, while 'to be' is a verb for existing that 'chopped' cuts down to LIV.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by name: Simón Bolívar, 'the Liberator', led the wars that freed much of South America from Spanish rule.

clue.text: Street Arab's original feature?

parts.note: the German prefix ur- means original or earliest, as in ur-text, the earliest version of a text
the chin is a feature of the face

explanation.surface: A question about what first made a ragged street child stand out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street Arab' is a dated, now offensive, term for a homeless child. The 's merely joins it to the wordplay, where 'original' gives the prefix UR-, as in ur-text.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated synonym, now considered offensive: both name a ragged, homeless child who lives on the city streets.

clue.text: After rising, I took meal, offering to respond in kind

indicators.note: this is a down entry, so a word that rises is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: later means after, at a subsequent time
taken as written
someone who took a meal ate

explanation.surface: Having got out of bed and eaten, the speaker proposes to return a favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After rising' reads as 'once I was up', but the two words do separate jobs: 'After' is a synonym, and 'rising', in a down clue, turns that synonym upwards to give RETAL. 'offering to' only links wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to pay someone back with the same treatment they gave you, usually returning harm for harm.

clue.text: Wind, storms and rain perhaps displacing river

indicators.note: to displace something is to shift it out of its place: the letter for the next word moves to another spot in the word before

parts.note: storms and rain are two examples of weather, and perhaps flags them as examples
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Gales, tempests and downpours force a river out of its course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' looks like moving air alongside the storms and rain, but it is the verb, as in winding a scarf round your neck. 'displacing' moves the R of WEATHER from the end up to second place.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to twist, coil or curl around something, as smoke or ivy does.

clue.text: Shameless, offering piece of music with random series of notes

parts.note: a bar is one of the short measures into which written music is divided
musical notes are named by the letters A to G; six of them are strung together here in no meaningful order

explanation.surface: A brazen performer presents a composition that is just notes thrown together anyhow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'random' tempts you to rearrange something, but the phrase is literal: six note names from A to G in no special order, E, F, A, C, E, D. 'offering' and 'with' only join the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe behaviour that is open and unashamed, as in a lie told with no sign of embarrassment.

clue.text: No progressive moves diluted

indicators.note: to move letters is to shift them about, so the word beside it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A report that none of the reforming measures was watered down.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'No progressive moves' together as a political phrase, but the definition ends after two words. 'moves' is the anagram signal for DILUTED; Luddites were English weavers who smashed new machinery around 1811.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive synonym: someone opposed to new technology or change, after the English textile workers who wrecked machinery in the 1810s.

clue.text: Assert power and scold, receiving incomplete order

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for power

indicators.note: the scolding word receives the next piece, taking it inside itself

parts.note: to rate someone is an old verb for telling them off angrily; it survives in berate

indicators.note: an incomplete word is one missing its last letter

parts.note: an edict is an official order or decree

explanation.surface: A bossy officer throws their weight about and tells people off after being handed only partial instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incomplete' cuts the order short, leaving EDIC, and 'receiving' is the container signal. The word for scold is an old verb that survives in 'berate', and the definition is a term from logic and grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal synonym: to affirm or state something as true of a subject, a sense used mainly in logic and grammar.

clue.text: Female firmness seen as unfriendliness

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female, as on forms
rigidity is stiffness, the quality of being firm and unbending

explanation.surface: A woman's resolve gets mistaken for coldness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen as' links the wordplay to the definition. The surface makes a wry point about how a resolute woman is judged.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a cold, stiff manner that shows no warmth towards other people.

clue.text: Made brisk manoeuvres to reach the shore

indicators.note: manoeuvres are movements, so the letters just before this word are moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters in all

explanation.surface: A crew steered smartly to bring their boat in to land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvres' is the anagram signal for MADE BRISK; in the surface it is simply what a boat's crew carries out.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym with a nautical slant: to leave a ship and go ashore at the end of a voyage.

clue.text: Bard, one writing in dialect, is a great hit in America

parts.note: Homer, the ancient Greek epic poet credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, was a bard
writers show dialect speech by spelling one as 'un, as in 'a good 'un'

explanation.surface: A poet who writes in regional speech turns out to be hugely popular in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one writing in dialect' means the word one as dialect spells it: 'un, as in 'a good 'un'. A home run is baseball's biggest hit, the ball struck so far that the batter circles all the bases.
explanation.definitionFit: Baseball term: a strike of the ball that lets the batter go round every base and score, baseball being America's national game.

clue.text: Flat's interior unfinished, but good to get in

indicators.note: the good word has to get in, that is go inside, the cut-short word before it
an unfinished word stops short, without its last letter

parts.note: the inside of something is its interior
pi is old British slang, short for pious, meaning sanctimoniously good

explanation.surface: The inside of an apartment still needs work, though it is nice enough to move into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' is not an apartment here but the adjective meaning dull or tasteless. 'unfinished' trims the word for interior to INSID, and 'to get in' is the container signal for a slang word, short for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: food or drink that is flat has lost its flavour or sparkle, and anything dull and lifeless can be called either.

clue.text: Old relative off to Scottish island

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old, as in OE for Old English
kin means family; someone who is kin to you is a relative
awa' is the Scots form of away, so it is what off, in the sense of away, is to a Scottish speaker

explanation.surface: An elderly family member sets off for an island off the coast of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish island' is a trap: 'Scottish' belongs with 'off to', giving AWA, the Scots for away, and the definition is just 'island'. Okinawa is a Japanese island in the East China Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: the largest of Japan's Ryukyu Islands, in the East China Sea.

clue.text: Shoots pianists, perhaps, missing piano

indicators.note: the word before is missing, that is lacks, the letter that the next word stands for

parts.note: pianists are one example of players, people who play an instrument; perhaps flags the example
p is the abbreviation for piano, the musical direction to play softly

explanation.surface: A gunman fires at the musicians, possibly, while his bullets fail to hit their instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoots' reads as a verb but is a noun: in gardening, layers are shoots pegged into the soil to root while still attached to the parent plant. 'missing' takes P, music's abbreviation for piano, off PLAYERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardening sense: stems pegged down into the soil so that they root while still attached to the parent plant.
